question_text:
The Feather and The Flint: When X first began going to the local school, the person who entered his name in the roster mistook his Muslim surname ______ for the more common Indian surname _____ and wrote it down that way. As a result, this became his official name and he did not take the trouble to rectify the matter in adulthood.
X became the junior national Badminton champion and the national champion in his first attempts. After that, he went on an unbelievable streak to win the national championship every single year between 1980 and 1987. In 1981, he received the Arjuna Award. At the 1982 Asian Games, he won the men's singles Bronze. The same year, he won the Men's singles Gold at the Commonwealth Games. With a dream career thus far, he was touted to be the next Indian sports icon.
An extremely discordant marriage led to a sudden dip in his form, losing the 1988 trophy. Two months later, he was shot dead in Lucknow as he came out of the K. D. Singh Babu Stadium after a practice session. The murder sent shockwaves through India, especially after the police filed murder charges against X's wife, and her lover (and future husband), a former RS member and Union Minister with Congress, who, in the most tragicomic sense, defected to BJP in 2019. Name X.

An Accent of Deception: James McAvoy, the Scottish actor and director, is going to make his directorial debut in April 2026 with a movie titled X. The movie, based on a true story, is about Silibil N' Brains, a Scottish hip-hop duo who famously posed as an American rapping duo to land a record deal. It is considered as one of the weirdest hoaxes in the hip-hop world.
In the early 2000s, the duo, Gavin and Billy, were working together in Scotland, but found that the idea of Scottish rap was not taken seriously in London. After being dismissed during auditions because of their accents, they decided to take on American identities, pretending to be from San Jacinto in California. Under their new identity, they were more successful at getting attention in London, eventually moving to the city to do the rounds performing live. They rapidly got management with Jonathan Shalit (who has managed the likes of Rebecca Ferguson, Simon Cowell, Cher, among others), a record deal with Sony Music UK for two singles and an album, and ended up appearing on MTV.
What is the title of this movie, an apt wordplay on a 1960s song that also featured in the movie 'Once Upon A Time In Hollywood', to hint at this phenomenal con-job?
answer_text: California Schemin' (based on John and Michelle Phillips' song California Dreamin')

question_text:
The Monopoly of Malice: This term originated in the 1560s and is a combination of two elements. The first part is derived from a French common-use word, while the second part probably stems from an old provincial English term for "huckster" or "cheat," which is believed to come from the name of a famous 15th-16th century German family of merchants and financiers in Augsburg.
This banking family replaced the Medici family who influenced all of Europe during the Renaissance. Alongside the Welsers, this family controlled much of the European economy in the 16th century, accumulated enormous wealth and held a near monopoly on the European copper market.
At the height of their power the family was sharply criticized by the contemporaries, especially by Martin Luther, for selling indulgences and benefices and urging the Pope to roll back the prohibition on the levying of interest. The imperial authorities in Nuremberg also brought strict action against them to halt their monopolistic practices. This controversy led to their name being used in common parlance for someone who cheated or manipulated.
Which term is being described here, that is often used for lawyers who deploy small yet effective methods that may deceive and manipulate people during arbitration?
answer_text: Pettifogging / Pettifogger (Petit + Fogger, based on the Fugger family)

question_text:
In the Secret Kitchen of the Babi: The Royal family of Balasinor traces their roots back to the Babi dynasty, originally a tribe of Pashtuns from Afghanistan who had ruled over parts of Gujarat. When the family decided to open the doors of their private palatial residence to guests, the rajmata took it upon herself to develop Balasinor as a culinary mecca for travellers.
For dinner, silver platters of roasts, shammi kebabs and dishes that sound too romantic to refuse, appear. Consider Murg-e-Alamgeer, named after Alamgir, another moniker for the great Mughal emperor Aurangzeb. Hariyali ki Nazakat, an ode to the elegance of greens. Motiya Kheer, a silken milk dessert of bottle gourd and sago balls that promises the sophistication of pearls.
But what stands out is this one dish X, a "jazzed up" version of the traditional Mughlai dish, Nargisi Kofta. It consists of a hard-boiled egg covered in a layer of savory mutton mince (kheema), which is then coated in chickpea flour (besan) and lightly fried. Invented by Nawabzadi Aaliya Sultana Babi, princess of the erstwhile princely state, the dish gets its name in honor of the unique identity of Balasinor in history, as it shot to global fame in 1980s upon discovery of certain relics.
What is the name of this dish, X?
answer_text: Dinosaur Eggs (a variation of Nargisi Kofta invented by the 'Dinosaur Princess' Aaliya Sultana Babi)

question_text:
A Gentleman's Truce on the Malecon: Among locations that have been on the F1 scene in history for a very brief time, X is one such example. A street circuit was established on the Malecon, a broad esplanade, roadway, and seawall that stretches for 8 km (5 miles) along the coast in X. The circuit saw races in 1957, 1958, and 1960.
The most rememberable race among the three was the 1958 Grand Prix, and strangely, it is remembered for something that happened before the race, off the circuit. Juan Manuel Fangio, the winner of the 1957 race, was abducted at gunpoint on the night of February 23 from his hotel. This was an attempt to sabotage the race and thereby draw international attention to the cause of challenging the authoritarian regime in X.
Fangio, who was 46 and the reigning F1 champion, was treated with immense respect by his captors. He was not harmed and was even described as "charmed" by his abductors. He was held for 29 hours and released unharmed shortly after the race concluded. Fascinating to say the least, he refused to identify his captors, later stating, "If what they did was in a good cause, then I, as an Argentine, accept it".
Id X.
answer_text: Havana, Cuba (Havana Grand Prix). Fangio was abducted by 26th July Movement rebels to challenge the portrayal of stability by dictator Batista.

question_text:
Inheritance of the Fall: X was a left revolutionary movement organized in Germany during World War I and immediately thereafter. It was founded in August 1914 as the International Group by Rosa Luxemburg, Karl Liebknecht, Clara Zetkin, and other members of the Social Democratic Party of Germany (SPD) who were dissatisfied with the party's servile compliance with the government's war policies. During the November Revolution of 1918 that broke out across Germany at the end of the war, the group re-established itself as a nationwide, non-party organization called X with the goal of instituting a council republic that would include all of Germany.
The movement's name referred to X, who is considered as a symbol of force against classicism and divide for his heroism as displayed in what is modern-day Bulgaria. For the group, his name symbolized the ongoing resistance of the oppressed against their exploiters and thus expressed the communist view of historical materialism, according to which history is driven by class struggles.
In 1919, the movement endorsed an armed uprising against the provisional government led by Friedrich Ebert of the Majority Social Democratic Party of Germany, which much like X, was suppressed and thoroughly defeated. Id X.
answer_text: Spartacus League / Spartacist League (named after Spartacus, leader of a famous slave revolt in ancient Rome, representing the fight against oppression)

question_text:
The Banal Commonality: What two-word phrase connects these unrelated events?
- In 1970, a group of young Vietnam war protestors found themselves in legal hot water when they were charged with "conspiracy to incite a riot" in the wake of a violent protest at a courthouse. The trial was quickly derailed by the defendants' vocal disruptions including catcalls directed at the judge, a protest walkout, and their eventual refusal to enter the courtroom. It was declared a mistrial, citing all defendants for contempt of court. They were summarily found as guilty of contempt, sentenced to six months in prison.
- In 1991, two years after the infamous Exxon Valdez spill, Exxon forced a quiet, separate financial settlement of damages with a group of seafood producers - Aleutian Dragon Fisheries (ADF), Icicle Seafoods, North Coast Seafood Processors, North Pacific Processors, Ocean Beauty Seafoods, Trident Seafoods and Wards Cove Packing Co. - for the disaster's effect on the Alaskan seafood industry. The out of court settlement granted only $63.75 million, compared to $750 million of actual award if all the plaintiffs had seen through the full trial.
answer_text: Seattle Seven (a group of radical anti-Vietnam War protesters associated with the Seattle Liberation Front, and also a group of seven seafood companies that negotiated a secret settlement with Exxon)

question_text: The Opportunity: Identify the moment in history when this photo was taken [a colorized photo of nine uniformed soldiers of different nationalities, including a Sikh soldier in a turban, standing in a row outside a building] - looking for some keywords.
answer_text: Eight-Nation Alliance / Boxer Rebellion (a multinational military coalition that invaded northern China in 1900 to suppress the Boxer Rebellion, entering Beijing in August 1900 and forcing Empress Dowager Cixi to flee)

question_text:
Maestro: Charanjit Singh was an Indian musician and composer. For over three decades, he was a core figure in Bollywood's music industry and a part of the inner creative circle of Kishore Kumar, Laxmikant-Pyarelal, and R. D. Burman, touring worldwide with them and shaping the sound of Hindi film music during its golden era.
He was widely recognized for introducing modern electronic textures into film orchestras, and was often called upon for guitar, bass, keyboards, and synthesizer parts. R. D. Burman frequently relied on Singh, with colleagues recalling that "if there was a modern sound Pancham Da wanted, Charanjit was often the first call."
However, Charanjit Singh is best known for an unprecedented 1982 work, created with Roland's then-new TB-303, TR-808, and Jupiter-8. Unfortunately, despite its pathbreaking nature, the album failed spectacularly, making it a forgotten gem.
But just like good work always finds its way to glory - this album was rediscovered in 2002 and re-issued in 2010, leading to tremendous international attention due to comparisons with X from the mid to late 1980s. Since then, certain commentators in the music press have recast Singh as an originator of X and the album to be a precursor to X, earning Singh the global recognition as the "father of X". What is X? A specific keyword carries all the points.
answer_text: Acid House Music (Charanjit Singh's 1982 album 'Synthesizing: Ten Ragas to a Disco Beat' is considered by some as the first ever acid house record)

question_text:
The Digital Messiah: AI "X": What Artificial Intelligence Can Do, What It Can't, and How to Tell the Difference is a 2024 non-fiction book written by scholars Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor. It is a critique of the tech industry's overly inflated promises and capabilities of artificial intelligence, as well as a debunking of the flawed beliefs fuelling AI hype.
Arvind Narayanan is a computer science professor at Princeton University, while Kapoor is a doctoral candidate. In 2023, Narayanan and Kapoor appeared on the TIME100 Artificial Intelligence list, which features influential figures in the field.
Narayanan and Kapoor argue that many individuals do not yet have the literacy to detect functioning aspects of AI similar to X, which they identify as "AI that does not and cannot work as advertised". Some of the major examples in the book include false powers of predictive AI, harm produced by GenAI, deepfakes and preservation of artistic property.
X is a term used to describe deceptive marketing, for any product with exaggerated marketing but questionable or unverifiable quality. X is also used in cryptography to refer to fraudulent methods and in mathematics for a method of summation of coefficients of a formal power series. What is being discussed here?
answer_text: Snake Oil (the book is 'AI Snake Oil')

question_text:
Clash of the Titans: The 1959 epic Ben-Hur is one of the biggest films in Hollywood history, and it has generated its share of outsized urban legends: A stuntman's death; a Ferrari zooming through a chariot race; a screenwriter faking a same-sex romance. But none of the legends are as crazy as those of the original Ben-Hur, a wildly expensive and unsafe 1925 production.
From the beginning, the film was cursed: Months of unsupervised shooting in Italy yielded terrible footage, prompting the studio to fire the crew. When filming resumed in Rome with new crew - fires on set; extras were reported missing; an elderly actor caught pneumonia; crew accidentally dug into an ancient Roman catacomb, destroying the 2000-year old site.
But what takes the cherry on top is what happened during the first big action sequence - a sea fight between a Roman war galley and a pirate ship. The casting director hired dozens of local peasants to play the ships' crews and divided them into two groups. Completely unprompted, suddenly the two groups started brawling with each other, so much that they destroyed the $80,000 ships on set, before the camera even began rolling. In a jiffy, the entire schedule & budget went bust.
Later, the casting director revealed he had divided the two groups in a particular way to add some realism to the conflict, that in those times, was a recipe for disaster. What classification might he have followed?
answer_text: Fascist / Anti-fascist factions of Italy (the casting director split the extras along the political fault lines of Mussolini-era Italy)

question_text:
We Could Have Had It All: The relationship between Sylvia Plath and Ted Hughes is one of the most intense, mythologized, and tragic in literary history. Plath met Ted in February 1956 at a party. She'd read some of Ted's poems and was very impressed. As soon as they met, the sparks flew, and when a couple hours later Ted leaned in to kiss her, she was so overwhelmed that she ended up biting him on the cheek. If anything, this violent, electric interaction marked the beginning of their passionate romance.
It took them only 4 months since this meeting, to impulsively decide to get married. And to little surprise, the two literary geniuses decided to honour their common favourite author X, by setting the date of wedding as 16th June. The day is a celebration of the life of X, observed annually by fans worldwide. The day is named after the protagonist of X's most famous 1922 work (title may remind you of a US president), whose events take place on 16 June 1904. Co-incidentally, X had also chosen to set his novel on this date as it was when he had the first romantic encounter with his wife-to-be.
It's just a shame that despite this impulsive yet romantic decision, Ted's infidelity, physical and emotional abuse brought down the marriage in just 4 years, leading Plath to commit suicide at the age of just 30. Who is the author X on whose happy day, these two walked unknowingly, into hell?
answer_text: James Joyce (Bloomsday, 16 June, named after Leopold Bloom, protagonist of Ulysses)

question_text:
The Sporting Spectacle (Gifted by: Abhishek Saluja): In 1999, ESPN's SportsCentury project ranked the Top 50 North American Athletes of the 20th century. Michael Jordan topped the list, followed by Babe Ruth, Muhammad Ali, Jim Brown, and Wayne Gretzky. At number 35 - sandwiched between Oscar Robertson and Mickey Mantle - sat X.
X's career lasted just sixteen months, during which X won 16 of 21 competitive outings. X's greatest performance came in June 1973, shattering a record that had stood for sixteen years and finishing so far ahead of the competition, that the margin of victory itself set a record that stands to this day. A commentator famously described X as "moving like a tremendous machine." That summer, X's face knocked the Watergate scandal off the cover of Time magazine. X also became the first athlete to appear on the covers of Time, Newsweek, and Sports Illustrated in the same week.
After X's death in 1989, a post-mortem revealed that X's heart weighed 22 pounds - more than twice the average.
In 2005, ESPN Classic's "Who's No. 1?" ranked the greatest individual athletic performances of all time. X's 1973 performance placed second, behind only Wilt Chamberlain's 100-point game. Id this generational athlete X.
answer_text: Secretariat (the champion American Thoroughbred who won the 1973 Triple Crown)

question_text:
True Detective: It all started when children of lawyer and private detective Francisco Marco, director of the Method3 agency - best-known business group dedicated to private research in Spain - gave him this challenge over a dinner table.
He started from his office in Barcelona. He turned to his sources and sent people to the field. Soon enough, the evidence emerged. The first one was the creation of a website domain in 2009, registered under the name of Robin Gunningham. Furthermore, a financial structure was uncovered, under a fictitious name David Jones ('co-incidentally' the real name of David Bowie), involving firms like Pest Control Office Ltd., Dismaland, Gross Domestic Product Ltd., & Picturesonwalls Ltd.
A key clue came from an arrest made in New York in 2000. The authorities charged a man accused of vandalism with a felony because the charges exceeded $1,500. However, the bail was posted, and the incident was largely buried, until an information from 2022 triangulated the evidence. Immigration records showed that a David Jones, crossed into Ukraine from Poland - the same time as Massive Attack frontman Robert Del Naja.
What was Francisco Marco and his Spanish intelligence agency investigating, which they eventually solved in 2026?
answer_text: Revealing the identity of Banksy (the leading theory links Banksy to Robin Gunningham, a 51-year-old from Bristol, confirmed by a major 2026 investigation)

question_text:
Twenty Thousand Stories under the Sea: 'Portrait d'une Femme' or 'Portrait of a Woman' by Ezra Pound is a clever poem about the history and power, or lack thereof, of the female muse in modern poetry. Think of the character Eloise from the TV show Bridgerton. It addresses an upper-class woman who decided to pursue social status and independence rather than a more conventional marriage.
The poem opens with a line: "Your mind and you are our Sargasso Sea.."
Sargasso Sea, in the North Atlantic region, historically, has been known as a "graveyard" for ships. Because the waters are so calm (the "horse latitudes"), sailing vessels would often get stuck there, mired in the floating seaweed (Sargassum), and the lack of wind, surrounded by the debris of other wrecked ships. So, when Pound writes that line, he is describing the woman's intellect as a vast, stagnant repository compared to a sea full of debris: she has collected interesting stories and ideas from important people, but has never developed a real identity of her own.
Literary comparables aside, what could be the reason behind Sargasso Sea being eerily quiet, especially in a tempestuous region like Northern Atlantic?
answer_text: It is the only sea in the world that has no coasts - bounded only by ocean currents (the Gulf Stream, North Atlantic, Canary, and North Atlantic Equatorial currents), creating a still vortex effect that traps water, seaweed and debris.

question_text:
The Philosophical Meme (Gifted by: Abhishek Saluja): Rahat Indori was a showman. At mushairas across India and the Gulf, where most poets recited from their seats in measured tones, Indori would leap to his feet, pause for effect, repeat his best couplets until the crowd demanded them again. He also wrote lyrics for Bollywood (including Munna Bhai MBBS and Mission Kashmir) but his heart belonged to the live circuit.
One of his signature couplets, "Sabhi ka khoon hai shaamil yahan ki mitti mein / Kisi ke baap ka Hindustan thodi hai," became an anthem during the 2019-20 protests against the Citizenship Amendment Act. But it was a different ghazal, one offering wry advice to the lovelorn, that would give him an unexpected second life online.
In early 2020, just weeks before the world locked down, TikTok users discovered an old clip of Indori reciting this ghazal. The opening line became a viral format, with lip-syncs and parodies flooding Instagram and Twitter during Valentine's Week. Commentators called it the "Sakht Launda 2.0" moment. Indori, then 70, found himself a meme.
He passed away later that year from COVID-19. But the meme outlived him, still used by anyone who wants to seem unbothered. Id this meme/line from his ghazal.
answer_text: "Bulaati Hai Magar Jaane Ka Nahi" (from a ghazal by Rahat Indori, a viral meme/line especially around Valentine's Day 2020)

question_text:
Tiebreaker 1: Norden Tenzing Bhutia was a Nepali musician, composer and singer of classic Nepali pop songs. In the 1970s Bhutia was the vocalist and guitarist of the very popular Nepali ensemble, The Himalayans. He is credited with transforming Nepali music and heralding a change in musical taste and content. Bhutia was one of the pioneers to introduce rock, pop and blues to Nepali mainstream music.
In 1999, unbeknownst to each other, childhood friends Vishal Dadlani and Shekhar Ravjiani were separately composing songs for the same film X, and coincidentally met in a studio where they decided to form the music director duo Vishal-Shekhar. Before that, Vishal Dadlani was composing music in a trio with Shiraz Bhattacharya (of Bombay Velvet and Phillauri fame) and Samrat.
Penned by Raj Kaushal, the director and producer of X, Vishal-Shiraz-Samrat adapted Norden Bhutia and The Himalayans' most popular song Y in Hindi, while retaining the opening lines in Nepali. Shaan made his Bollywood debut with this song, which went onto become a popular romantic number over the years, while the movie gradually faded out from public memory. Id the movie X and the song Y.
answer_text: X = Pyaar Mein Kabhi Kabhi; Y = Musu Musu Haasi Deu Malai Lai

question_text:
Tiebreaker 2: X was a niece of Rabindranath Tagore and among the first women to graduate from Calcutta University, winning the Padmavati Gold Medal in 1890. She is credited with setting "Vande Mataram" to music. In 1910, she founded Bharat Stree Mahamandal in Allahabad - the first national-level women's organisation in India.
In 1919, Y visited Lahore for the first time and stayed at X's home while her husband was imprisoned for his role in the Rowlatt Satyagraha. A close friendship developed. Over the following months, the two exchanged letters at a feverish pace - at one point, Y sent 25 letters in 16 days. Y referred to their bond as a "spiritual marriage" and wrote to a friend: "Our relation is beyond definition." In one letter to X, Y confessed: "You still continue to haunt me even in my sleep."
The relationship eventually cooled, reportedly after intervention from C. Rajagopalachari. Years later, in 1936, Y told the American birth control advocate Margaret Sanger that he had once "nearly slipped" with a woman of "broad cultural education" but had been "saved" by those around him.
X and Y both passed away before seeing what fate had in store: X's only son married the daughter of Y's cousin. Id X and Y.
answer_text: X = Sarla Devi Chaudhurani; Y = Mahatma Gandhi
